tests.name: scan_size
tests.title: Test 1 — Scan: haystack size (needle at the end)
tests.description: A plain literal search for a single needle occurring once, with the needle at the very end of the text — the worst case, the whole haystack must be scanned. Variable: haystack size from 64 KB to 16 MB. This is the classic log-grep workload: rurex scans with SIMD-accelerated prefilters, `re` steps its backtracking VM character by character.
tests.data_example: text fox the value lorem dog dog jumps value fox line value code gamma brown delta hello quick the brown lazy …

sweeps.label: haystack size, needle at the end (worst case)

tests.name: scan_position
tests.title: Test 2 — Scan: needle position (fixed 8 MB haystack)
tests.description: The same single-needle literal search as Test 1, but the haystack is fixed at 8 MB and the variable is where in the text the needle sits, from the first bytes (0%) to the very end (100%). Position 0% favors `re`'s instant fast path; every later position is scan-bound.
tests.data_example: data data quick brown brown sit path over value node line da … the-needle-string dog delta gamma jumps sit rust omega alpha text delta brown …

sweeps.label: needle position in the fixed 8 MB haystack

tests.name: extract_size
tests.title: Test 3 — Extraction: haystack size (fixed density, 80 matches/KB)
tests.description: Digit-run extraction (`findall`) over word filler at a fixed density of 80 matches per KB. Variable: haystack size from 64 KB to 4 MB (the match count grows with it). This is the match-dense regime, where building Python match objects — not scanning — dominates.
tests.data_example: 7685 6216 word 2369 beta 205 5643 value 7697 value 1424 word 9181 770 node 6309 beta 7505 7023 beta 2859 beta …

sweeps.label: haystack size at fixed density (80 matches/KB)

tests.name: extract_density
tests.title: Test 4 — Extraction: match density (fixed 1 MB haystack)
tests.description: The same digit-run extraction as Test 3, but the haystack is fixed at 1 MB and the variable is match density, from 5 to 160 matches per KB. This isolates the per-match cost from the scan cost and shows the crossover: sparse matches are scan-bound (rurex territory), dense matches are extraction-bound (`re` territory).

sweeps.label: match density in the fixed 1 MB haystack

tests.name: pathological
tests.title: Test 5 — Pathological: catastrophic backtracking
tests.description: The pattern `(x+x+)+y` never matches a run of x's, and for a backtracking engine the number of ways to distribute the x's across the groups grows exponentially: `re`'s time doubles with every two extra characters. A finite-automata engine cannot backtrack, so rurex' time is flat. This is a safety property (ReDoS resistance), not a speed feature.
tests.data_example: xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx  (n = 24 of the sweep; no y, so nothing matches)
